title: Buying Dye Material by the Pound
summary: A pound of root bark dyes roughly one to two pounds of wool at useful depth, and two or three times that if you work the exhaust baths. Buying one larger batch also keeps colour consistent across a run, which matters more than the saving for anyone selling finished work.
body: Two reasons to buy a pound rather than an ounce, and the second one is the one that catches people out.
## What a pound actually dyes

| Depth | Bark as % of fibre | Fibre from 1 lb of bark |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deep | 100% | About 1 lb |
| Mid | 50 to 75% | 1⅓ to 2 lb |
| Pale | 25 to 40% | 2½ to 4 lb |
| Plus exhaust baths | — | Add roughly half again |

So a pound covers a sizeable project: a sweater's worth of yarn at depth, or three or four graded skeins if you work the [second and third baths](/blog/getting-a-second-and-third-bath-from-one-batch).
## Batch consistency is the real argument

Bark from different harvests varies in tone. In a single dye pot that is invisible. Across a run of twenty skeins dyed over three months from three different purchases, it is obvious on the shelf — and a customer who bought two skeins to knit one garment will see it before you do.

One larger batch, dyed from the same material with the same recorded ratios, is how a small maker gets pieces that match. It is the same reason soap makers keep to one batch of colourant across a run.
## Storage is the constraint, not the price

A pound only makes sense if it survives. Kept dry, dark and sealed, this material holds its colour strength for years; kept in a damp garage it cakes and goes musty in a season. See [storing root bark so it lasts](/blog/storing-root-bark-so-it-lasts).
Buy the cut you can store. Powder needs an airtight container and is unforgiving of damp; shredded and stripped material is far more tolerant of an imperfect cupboard.
## Planning a quantity

1. Weigh the dry fibre for the whole project, including the bits you have not started.
2. Decide the depth, and take the percentage from the table above.
3. Add a quarter for test pots. Every batch should be tested before it meets the good fibre.
4. Round up to a size that stores cleanly rather than one that leaves an awkward remainder.
## What this material is not

Everything described here is raw botanical material sold for dyeing, soap making and craft work. It is not food, it is not a supplement, and it is not for human consumption. Nothing on this page is a recommendation to put any of it in or on a body.

title: Working Safely With Fine Milled Bark
summary: Any finely milled plant material makes an airborne dust that irritates eyes, nose and airways. Open the bag at waist height in still air, wear a fitted P2 or N95 mask when weighing or milling, wipe surfaces damp rather than sweeping, and keep it away from food areas and pets.
body: This is the least interesting article on the site and the one most worth reading before your first pound of powder arrives. Fine botanical dust is a nuisance and an irritant, and every measure below is ordinary workshop practice rather than anything dramatic.
## Why powder needs more care than bark

Milling multiplies surface area, which is exactly why powder dyes faster — and it is the same property that puts material into the air. A shredded bark barely raises dust. An opened bag of fine powder in a draught will coat a room.
## The short list

- **Open the bag low and slowly**, at waist height, away from your face, in still air. Not under a ceiling fan, not beside an open window with a breeze.
- **Wear a fitted mask** — P2 or N95 — for weighing, milling or anything that stirs the material up. A loose surgical mask does nothing for dust.
- **Wear eye protection** while milling. Dust in the eye is the most common complaint by a wide margin.
- **Gloves** keep it off your hands and out of everything you touch next. Tannin stains skin for a day or two.
- **Wipe up damp.** Sweeping puts settled dust back into the air; a damp cloth ends the problem.
- **Keep it out of the kitchen.** Separate pots, separate scales, separate surfaces. Store it away from food, children and animals.
## Ventilation

Work where air moves gently and away from you — a garage with the door open, a bench near a window with an extractor. Still air is better than a draught that lifts the dust, and both are better than a small closed room.
## If you are milling it yourself

Milling is where the dust is worst. Let the grinder stand for a minute after it stops so the cloud inside settles before you open it, and do it outdoors if you can. See [milling your own powder at home](/blog/milling-your-own-powder-at-home).
## Spills

Do not vacuum a spill with a household vacuum: most of them pass fine dust straight through the exhaust and distribute it. Damp paper towel, then a damp wipe of the area, then wash the cloth separately.

title: Milling Your Own Powder From Bark
summary: A coffee or spice grinder will take shredded bark to a usable powder in short bursts, sieved between passes. It is worth doing when you want one cut in the cupboard and both in the pot; it is not worth doing for volume, because domestic grinders overheat and the dust is considerable.
body: Buying shredded bark and milling what you need gives you both cuts from one purchase. Shredded stores better, re-baths better and is easier to strain; powder loads a bath fast. Milling in small amounts lets you choose per project.
## What works

| Tool | Verdict |
| --- | --- |
| Blade coffee or spice grinder | Best domestic option. Short bursts, small loads. |
| Blender | Chops rather than mills; fine for a coarse grind only. |
| Burr coffee grinder | Avoid — fibrous bark jams the burrs. |
| Mortar and pestle | Works, slowly, for very small amounts. |
| Hammer mill | The right tool, and rarely worth owning for this. |
Keep a grinder for this and do not use it for food afterwards. Tannin and aroma both persist.
## Method

1. Start with **dry** material. Anything damp gums the chamber and mills to a paste.
2. Break long pieces down by hand or with shears first.
3. Load **no more than a third full**.
4. Run in **five-second bursts**, shaking the grinder between them. Continuous running heats the material and the motor.
5. **Sieve** through a kitchen strainer. Return the coarse fraction for another pass.
6. Let the dust settle for a minute before opening the lid.
Two or three passes gives a powder fine enough for a dye bath. For soap you want it finer still — sieve through a very fine mesh and re-mill whatever will not pass.
## Heat is what spoils it

A grinder run continuously gets hot enough to smell, and a scorched batch dyes browner than it should. If the chamber is warm to the touch, stop and let it cool. The five-second rule exists for this reason, not to protect the motor.
## Dust

Milling is the dustiest thing you will do with this material. Mask, eye protection, outdoors or by an open door, and a damp wipe afterwards. See [working safely with fine milled bark](/blog/working-safely-with-fine-milled-bark).
## When to just buy powder

If you need more than a few ounces, buy it milled. A domestic grinder does perhaps two ounces before it needs a rest, the particle size is less even than a proper mill gives, and uneven particle size is exactly what makes a bath unpredictable. See [why particle size changes everything in a dye pot](/blog/why-particle-size-changes-everything-in-a-dye-pot).

title: Sassafras Albidum, a North American Dye Tree
summary: Sassafras albidum is a small deciduous tree of eastern North America, recognised by three leaf shapes on the same branch: unlobed oval, two-lobed mitten and three-lobed. Its aromatic root bark is used by dyers for rose-tan and orange-brown shades, and greys with an iron modifier.
body: Two different trees, two different continents, two different colours. Sassafras is not a substitute for mimosa root bark and does not behave like it, so it is worth knowing on its own terms.
## The tree

Sassafras albidum is a deciduous tree of the laurel family, native to eastern North America — broadly from southern Ontario and Maine down to Florida and west to Texas. It is usually a small tree of twenty to sixty feet, often growing in thickets at the edges of woodland and along fence lines, and it spreads readily from root suckers.
## How it is identified
The leaves are the giveaway, because one tree carries three shapes at once:

- **Unlobed** — a plain oval.
- **Two-lobed** — the mitten, with a thumb on one side.
- **Three-lobed** — a broad trident.

All three appear on the same branch, which almost nothing else does. Add the bright yellow-to-orange autumn colour, the green twigs, and the aroma when a twig or root is scratched, and identification is straightforward.
## What dyers get from it

| Mordant or modifier | Typical shade on wool |
| --- | --- |
| Alum | Rose-tan, warm apricot, soft orange-brown |
| No mordant | Weak, uneven — mordant it |
| Iron | Grey-brown to slate, muted |
| Alkali shift | Warmer, redder |

It sits in a different part of the colour wheel from mimosa root bark, which runs purple to maroon, and the two overdye well precisely because of that. A pale sassafras ground under a short mimosa bath gives a warm plum that neither material reaches alone.

Method is the same as any tannin bark: scour, mordant with alum, cold soak overnight, hold the bath at about 80°C rather than boiling it, and strain before the fibre enters. See [mordanting wool before a bark bath](/blog/mordanting-wool-before-a-bark-bath).
## Two honest notes
**Colour varies more than mimosa's does.** Root, root bark, bark and twig all give different strengths, and season affects it. Test every batch before committing good fibre.
**It is sold here as a dye material.** We make no claim about any other use, historical or otherwise, and nothing about this species is offered as a food, a flavouring or a supplement.
## What this material is not

Everything described here is raw botanical material sold for dyeing, soap making and craft work. It is not food, it is not a supplement, and it is not for human consumption. Nothing on this page is a recommendation to put any of it in or on a body.
